a.prompt: "Hi Mum, I dropped my phone, this is my new number. Please pay this bill urgently, I'll explain later." The profile photo is your child's. What first?
options: Call your child on their old, saved number to confirm
Send the money, it's an emergency
Ask them to send a selfie
Reply asking them to share the bank details
a.why: Scammers copy public photos. Confirm through a channel you already trust, like the old number, before sending anything.

b.prompt: Your 'manager' messages from an unsaved number: "In a meeting, can't talk. Buy 5 gift cards for a client and send me the codes." What do you do?
options: Buy them, then confirm later
Ask for the codes to be sent to a company email first
Verify with your manager via a known number or in person before doing anything
Buy just one card to be safe
b.why: Boss impersonation relies on secrecy and urgency. Gift-card codes are untraceable, so verify first through a trusted channel.

a.prompt: A friend's WhatsApp asks: "I sent you a 6-digit code by mistake, please forward it to me." What is this?
options: A harmless mix-up, forward the code
An attempt to take over your WhatsApp account
A bug in WhatsApp
A way to verify the friend's identity
a.why: That code is your own WhatsApp login code. Anyone holding it can register your number on their device.

task.intro: Swipe each message: scam or safe?

cards.text: "Hey! I accidentally sent my WhatsApp code to your number. Can you read it out to me?"
SMS you asked for while setting up a new phone: "Your WhatsApp code is 482-913. Don't share this code."
"I'm locked out of my account. Forward me the 6-digit code you just got, I'll explain later."
WhatsApp tip: "Turn on two-step verification in Settings > Account for extra protection."

b.prompt: You receive an unexpected WhatsApp verification SMS, then a contact messages: "Sorry, wrong number, can you read me the code?" What should you do?
options: Read it out, it's polite
Share it but change your password afterwards
Reply with only the last 3 digits
Never share it, and tell the contact to use another route
b.why: Verification codes must never be shared, in full or in part. A contact asking is likely already compromised.

task.intro: Swipe each message: scam or safe?

cards.text: "Sorry, wrong number! A code is coming to you from me. Can you share it back?"
SMS after you reinstalled WhatsApp yourself: "Use 731-205 to register. Never share this code."
Your friend's account: "I'm stuck! Read me the verification SMS you just got, quick!"
WhatsApp help page: "WhatsApp will never call or message to ask for your code."

a.prompt: You're added to a WhatsApp group where members post screenshots of daily stock profits and an 'expert' urges you to install an app to join an IPO quota. What's the smartest move?
options: Join with a small amount
Ask the expert for their experience
Leave the group, don't install the app, and report it
Wait to see if members really profit
a.why: Fake members and fabricated screenshots create social proof. Unregistered apps let scammers show fake gains while taking your deposits.

task.intro: Tap every red flag in this WhatsApp group message.

segments.t: Hello, you have been added to the
VIP Stock Club, a group you never asked to join
. Members earn
guaranteed 40% returns in 10 days
. Install our app
from this link instead of the Play Store
and deposit ₹10,000 to get an IPO quota.
Only 3 seats left, decide in 15 minutes!
Please see the details above.

b.prompt: A 'crypto signals' group promises guaranteed 3x returns in 30 days if you deposit through their platform. Which fact most clearly marks this as a scam?
options: Guaranteed high returns
The group has many members
The admin is friendly
Payments are made online
b.why: No legitimate investment can guarantee high returns. Guarantees, pressure and pooled unregulated platforms signal fraud.

task.intro: Tap every red flag in this WhatsApp group message.

segments.t: Welcome to Crypto Gold Signals!
We guarantee 3x your money in 30 days.
Transfer your deposit to
our private wallet, not a registered exchange
Screenshots of members' profits are posted below as proof.
Our manager will guide you step by step.
Offer ends tonight, no refunds.

a.prompt: Which of these is most likely the genuine Amazon India website?
options: amazon-in-support.com
amazon.in.secure-login.net
arnazon.in
amazon.in
a.why: Read the domain from right to left up to the first slash. The brand must be the registered domain, and lookalikes like 'arnazon' swap characters.

b.prompt: Which URL is most likely the genuine Flipkart site?
options: flipkart-offers.shop
flipkart.com
flipkart.com.deals-today.in
fIipkart.com
b.why: Extra words, odd endings or subdomain tricks can hide a fake registered domain. Stick to the exact brand domain.

a.prompt: At a café you notice the payment QR code is a sticker placed over the original one. What should you do?
options: Ask the staff to confirm and check the merchant name shown before paying
Scan it, since it's the café's code
Pay a small test amount
Scan it with a different app
a.why: Scammers paste their own QR codes over genuine ones. Confirm with staff and check the payee name before paying.

b.prompt: An email says: "Scan the QR code to re-enable your account's two-factor authentication." What do you do?
options: Scan with your phone's camera
Scan but don't log in
Don't scan, and check settings in the official app instead
Print it and scan on another phone
b.why: QR codes hide the destination from email filters and from you. Make security changes only inside the official app or site.

a.prompt: A caller says: "I'm from your bank. A ₹40,000 transaction is pending, share the OTP now to cancel it." What is the correct response?
options: Share the OTP to cancel the transaction
Hang up and call the number on your card or bank's official site
Share only 3 digits
Ask the caller for their employee ID
a.why: An OTP authorises a payment, it never cancels one. Banks never ask for OTPs. Calling back via official numbers verifies the claim.

task.intro: Match each caller's line to the right response. Tap a line, then its response.
left: "I'm from your bank. Read me the OTP to cancel a payment."
"Courier here. Tell me the OTP to confirm delivery."
"Your account freezes unless you share the CVV now."
"Tech support: install a remote app so I can fix this."
right: Hang up and call the number on your card
Refuse: a parcel never needs your OTP
Never share card details, end the call
Decline and use the official app or store

b.prompt: A 'delivery agent' calls and asks you to read out the OTP you just received 'to confirm the delivery'. You aren't sure what order it's for. What do you do?
options: Read it out
Read it out after verifying the agent's name
Ask them to send it as a text
Refuse, since OTPs are never needed to receive a parcel
b.why: Genuine OTP-based delivery codes are rare and tied to your order. If you can't tell, treat it as theft and don't share.

task.intro: Match each caller's line to the right response. Tap a line, then its response.
left: "Sir, a ₹40,000 debit is pending. Share the OTP to stop it."
"Madam, I'm your relationship manager. Confirm your card PIN."
"You won a gift! Tell me the SMS code to claim it."
"Telecom KYC expired. Share the code we just sent."
right: An OTP approves payments, it never cancels them
Banks never ask for your PIN
Real prizes never need your SMS code
Visit the operator's store or app instead

a.prompt: You're selling a sofa online. The buyer says: "I've sent you the money, approve the request on your UPI app and enter your PIN to receive it." What's wrong?
options: Nothing, that's how UPI works
The buyer used the wrong app
Entering a PIN sends money out, receiving money never needs a PIN
The request has expired
a.why: You never enter a UPI PIN to receive money. A collect request with a PIN prompt is pulling money out of your account.

task.intro: Swipe each UPI situation: scam or safe?

cards.text: A buyer says: "Approve the request on your app and enter your PIN to receive my payment."
You scan a shop's QR code and enter your own PIN to pay ₹250 for groceries.
A seller says: "I sent your refund. Just enter your UPI PIN to accept it."
You get a bank SMS showing a credit for money a friend sent you.

b.prompt: A seller says they've sent you a refund via a UPI 'request'. You see a prompt asking you to enter your UPI PIN. What do you do?
options: Decline the request and don't enter your PIN
Enter the PIN to get the refund
Enter the PIN but check the amount first
Ask the seller to try again
b.why: Refunds are credited automatically. A PIN prompt means money is leaving your account.

task.intro: Swipe each UPI situation: scam or safe?

cards.text: A stranger says: "Send ₹1 and enter your PIN to verify and win ₹5,000."
You type your PIN in your own UPI app to pay your electricity bill.
Someone says they paid you by mistake and sends a collect request asking you to pay them back.
A customer shows a payment screen, so you check your own bank app before handing over goods.

a.prompt: A 'support executive' asks you to install AnyDesk so they can 'fix your refund'. What happens if you do?
options: Nothing, it's only a chat tool
They can only see your photos
It just checks your internet speed
They can see and control your phone, including banking apps
a.why: Remote-access tools let scammers watch your screen, see OTPs and move money themselves.

task.intro: Tap every red flag in this 'support' call script.

segments.t: Hello sir, I am calling from the Refund Department. Your refund of ₹4,999 is stuck. To release it, please
install AnyDesk and read me the 9-digit code
. Keep your banking app open
so I can see your account
. When the bank sends an OTP,
read it out to me immediately
. Please
don't end the call or tell anyone
until it is done.

b.prompt: A caller claiming to be from your telecom provider says KYC has expired and asks you to share your screen via a quick-support app. Best action?
options: Share the screen but not the OTP
Decline, and visit the operator's store or official app
Share the screen while on loudspeaker
Share only for a minute
b.why: No legitimate service needs remote control of your phone for KYC. Visit the official store or app instead.

task.intro: Tap every red flag in this 'telecom' call script.

segments.t: Madam, this is TeleCare calling. Your SIM KYC has expired and
your number will be blocked in 30 minutes
. To fix it,
download the QuickSupport app and let me see your screen
. I will
also need the OTP that arrives
to update your records. You can
pay a ₹10 verification fee to my personal UPI number
to finish.

a.prompt: On a video call, a person in uniform says a parcel in your name contains illegal items, that you're under 'digital arrest', and must stay on camera and transfer money for 'verification'. What is this?
options: A scam: no agency arrests or investigates people by video call and demands money
A real police process
A court notice
A routine bank check
a.why: 'Digital arrest' doesn't exist in law. Agencies don't demand payments or isolation over a call. Disconnect and report to 1930.

task.intro: Match each caller's claim to the truth. Tap a claim, then the truth.
left: "Stay on camera and tell no one."
"Transfer money to a safe account to prove your innocence."
"I'll send my officer ID on WhatsApp."
right: Not a real legal process: hang up
Isolation and secrecy are scam tactics
Agencies never ask you to pay or move savings
Uniform photos and IDs are easy to fake

b.prompt: A caller says they're from TRAI and your number will be disconnected for illegal activity, then connects you to a 'police officer' who tells you not to tell anyone and to move your savings 'for safety'. What do you do?
options: Follow instructions, to avoid arrest
Move only part of your money
Hang up, tell family, and report at 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in
Ask them to send a letter by post
b.why: Secrecy and pressure are core scam tactics. Real authorities don't ask you to transfer money to prove innocence.

task.intro: Match each caller's claim to the truth. Tap a claim, then the truth.
left: "A parcel in your name has drugs."
"Your Aadhaar is linked to money laundering."
"Don't hang up or a warrant will be issued."
"Pay a fine now to close the case."
right: Scammers invent cases to scare you: check with the real agency
Authorities never investigate by video call
Keeping you on the line stops you from thinking or asking family
Courts don't collect fines over a phone call

a.prompt: Which combination of signs most strongly suggests a scam?
options: A greeting and a company logo
Urgency, secrecy and a request for money or codes
A message sent late at night
A message with a typo
a.why: Pressure to act fast, keep quiet and hand over money or codes is the common thread across scam types.

b.prompt: Which of these should make you most suspicious of a message?
options: It comes from a contact you've saved
It includes your first name
It has a link to a well-known brand
It offers a prize and says 'claim in the next 10 minutes, don't tell anyone'
b.why: Time pressure and secrecy stop you from checking with others. Slow down and verify.

questions.objective: Verifying identity through a second channel

a.prompt: A relative's WhatsApp account messages you asking for urgent money. What is the most reliable way to check?
options: Ask a personal question in the same chat
Check their profile photo
Call them on a number you already know
Ask them to send a voice note
a.why: If the account is hijacked, everything in that chat is controlled by the scammer. Use a separate, trusted channel.

task.intro: A relative's account asks for urgent money. Put the steps in the right order.
steps: Pause and don't send anything yet
Call them on a number you already have saved
Ask something only the real person would know
Send money only after confirming it's really them

b.prompt: A caller says they're from your bank. How do you confirm it?
options: Hang up and dial the number printed on your card or the bank's website
Trust the caller ID on your screen
Ask the caller to verify your details
Ask them to call back in an hour
b.why: Caller ID can be faked. Call the official number yourself to reach the real bank.

task.intro: A caller says they're from your bank. Put the steps in the right order.
steps: Don't share anything, just hang up
Find the bank's number on your card or its website
Act only through the bank's official channel

a.prompt: You've just lost money in an online scam. What is the best first step?
options: Wait a week to see if it's refunded
Post about it and wait for replies
Message the scammer to ask for a refund
Call the national cybercrime helpline 1930 and report at cybercrime.gov.in quickly
a.why: Fast reporting improves the chance of freezing funds. The helpline is 1930 and complaints are filed at cybercrime.gov.in.

task.intro: You've just been scammed. Put your response in order, most urgent first.
steps: Call your bank to block the account or card
Save screenshots and change your passwords

b.prompt: You realise you shared your OTP with a fraudster and money has left your account. What do you do first?
options: Wait for the bank to notice
Contact your bank to block the account or card, and report to 1930
Delete the chat
Change your phone wallpaper
b.why: Speed is critical. Alert your bank so it can block transactions, and report to the cybercrime helpline.

task.intro: You shared an OTP and money left your account. Most urgent first.
steps: Tell your bank immediately to block transactions
Note the transaction details and file at cybercrime.gov.in
Change passwords and warn family and friends
